problem: VLN-CE agents built on a waypoint predictor are trained only with high-level view selection and rely on an offline controller for low-level movement, so they ignore spatial information in low-level actions and perform poorly when made to output low-level actions. Existing waypoint predictors also use only RGB/depth features and ignore object semantics and passability (e.g. walls are impassable).
motivation: Real robots execute low-level controls, and the large performance drop from high-level to low-level action prediction shows a gap between visual perception and executed actions. Rich object semantics and prior knowledge about which objects are passable should help produce more feasible waypoints.
key_idea: Jointly train a Transformer text decoder that generates low-level action sequences alongside high-level viewpoint selection (dual-action), and improve the waypoint predictor with CLIP features plus an obstacle mask built from semantic segmentation and an open-area vocabulary.
insight: Low-level action supervision derived from the selected view improves both low-level navigation (WP-HAMT SR 0.35 to 0.43 with only the dual-action module) and high-level navigation when combined with the better waypoint predictor. CLIP features and the obstacle mask increase the share of predicted waypoints in open space (0.80 to 0.83 to 0.85). Semantic-rich features are not automatically better: InternVideo features hurt the waypoint predictor (0.65 open).
method: Obstacle-aware waypoint predictor: replaces ResNet-152 features with CLIP ViT-B/16 features (best among CLIP, DenseCLIP, InternVideo) and feeds them with depth to the Transformer waypoint predictor, which outputs a 120-angle by 12-distance heatmap.
Obstacle mask: uses MP3D semantic segmentation (~40 categories) and keeps only an open-area vocabulary (floor, stairs, doors) as 1, masking all other segments to 0 before waypoint prediction.

Low-level action decoder: a Transformer text decoder prompted with 'low actions:' takes the navigator's CLS representation and generates a sequence of LEFT/RIGHT/FORWARD tokens auto-regressively (max length 30, comma as end token).

Low-level label generation: for each selected high-level view, heading difference divided by 15 degrees gives the number of turns (smaller rotation direction) and distance divided by 0.25 m gives the number of FORWARD steps; remainders are dropped.

Joint training: L = L_high (IL+RL mixture with lambda 0.75) + L_low (token likelihood); inference uses greedy view selection for high-level and beam search (size 3) for low-level, with no waypoint predictor needed at low level.
Model-agnostic integration: applied on top of WP-VLN-BERT, WP-HAMT and ETPNav.

setting.backbone: WP-HAMT (InternVideo base visual encoder, BERT text encoder, DD-PPO depth) with a Transformer low-level decoder; also WP-VLN-BERT and ETPNav; CLIP ViT-B/16 waypoint predictor (trained)
setting.training_data: R2R-CE train split (61 MP3D scenes); waypoint predictor trained on the MP3D connectivity graph; low-level labels derived from selected views; no extra data reported
setting.observation: panoramic RGB (12 views) + depth; MP3D semantic segmentation used for the obstacle mask
setting.action_space: high-level: waypoint viewpoint selection (offline controller); low-level: FORWARD 0.25 m / TURN LEFT-RIGHT 15° / STOP
setting.privileged: MP3D ground-truth semantic segmentation is used to build the obstacle mask (train, and apparently at test for waypoint prediction)

numbers_note: All metrics are printed as fractions (0-1) in the paper and are reported as printed, not scaled to percent. No low-level test-unseen results.
results: The method improves all three baselines on high-level actions: WP-HAMT reaches SR 0.54 / SPL 0.49 on val-unseen (from 0.52 / 0.47) and SR 0.52 on test-unseen (from 0.49), and ETPNav reaches SR 0.58 on val-unseen (from 0.57). On low-level actions, WP-HAMT improves from SR 0.35 / SPL 0.32 to 0.44 / 0.38 and ETPNav+Ours reaches SR 0.48 / SPL 0.42, above LSTM-based low-level agents such as WS-MGMap (SR 0.39).
limitations: The low-level decoder increases computational cost.
A performance gap remains between low-level and high-level action navigation.
The obstacle mask relies on simulator ground-truth semantic segmentation, and generated low-level sequences sometimes reach the goal without following the instruction.
